report:
(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

Executive summary

At 02:47:12 on 12/08/2026 a 220 t class rigid haul truck, HT-407, descending the main ramp of the Stage 4 open pit at Bindarra Gold Mine empty, struck the right side of a light vehicle, LV-118, coming out of the RL 312 dewatering spur. Times in this report are local time (UTC+8). The truck had braked from 37 km/h to 24 km/h. It pushed the light vehicle 18.4 m down the ramp and rolled it onto its left side against the inner windrow. The sole occupant, a grade control technician employed by a survey subcontractor and on the third night shift at the mine, was conscious throughout. The technician was extricated through the rear at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision, and flown out at 07:40 with a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax. The light vehicle was destroyed. The truck was damaged at the front left and returned to service on 14/08/2026. The Stage 4 pit stood down for 9 hours 15 minutes, and the main ramp below RL 340 was closed for 22 hours. [NOT ESTABLISHED: injury status of the haul truck operator]

Neither driver knew of the other until the truck came over the crest. The survey gave 41 m of sight distance at the spur against a 96 m stopping distance, so the beacon was first in view at 53 m, six seconds before impact, and the truck could not stop in the distance available.

The spur was opened under works order WO-26-4471 as routine earthworks, so ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3 removed the management of change record and its three referrals, and this very likely contributed to the two gaps that followed. No stop control or warning sign was fitted although the intersection failed the sight distance rule, which likely contributed to the light vehicle driving out without stopping. Operators did not know that the S4-LOAD geofence suppressed the collision awareness system at the spur. On balance this likely contributed to neither driver being aware of the other, although the alert would have sounded only about a second before the brakes went on. The plan required a call only at nine listed intersections and the spur was not one, which very likely contributed to neither driver calling. Access cards were issued with no check of the pit driving assessment, which likely contributed to the light vehicle's exit from the spur. MSG-14 sets no review trigger and no basis for choosing positive-call intersections, and it likely made inaction the default, although the mine could have acted on its own. This and the geofence judgement are held at the standard of proof and no higher.

Several defences worked. The haul truck operator responded within 1.4 seconds, inside the 1.5 seconds the plan allows, and braked at 0.78 m/s2 net against the unit's tested 0.80. The roll-over protection structure was not breached and the seatbelt was worn.

The Mining Manager issued a site-wide direction at 05:10 on 12/08/2026 requiring a call before entering any Stage 4 intersection, and the spur was barricaded and closed. Survey found two of ten other unlisted Stage 4 roads below the clause 6.2 minimum, and both were closed pending a stop control. Suppressed proximity events were added to the monthly collision awareness report on 28/08/2026. Three recommendations to the mine remain open, on works order classification, the plan's route to Appendix B, and geofence changes.

Two matters were examined without conclusion. The evidence on airborne dust affecting the haul truck operator's sighting is evenly balanced, as is the evidence on operator fatigue. The nine minute wait for the second responder during extrication is a separate matter, still being examined, and is described as a risk on every night shift.

Event overview

This section describes what happened, in the order it happened.

Occurrence particulars

At 02:47:12 on 12/08/2026, a 220 t class rigid haul truck, HT-407, descending the main ramp of the Stage 4 open pit at Bindarra Gold Mine struck the right side of a light vehicle, LV-118, at the RL 312 dewatering spur intersection. The light vehicle driver, a grade control technician employed by the survey subcontractor Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical, was seriously injured. The occurrence was notified as ORR-OCC-2026-0332, raised at 03:26 on 12/08/2026, and was reported to the State Mines Inspectorate as a reportable injury.

Three organisations were involved. Orrabinda Resources operates the mine, and its Mining Manager owns the traffic management plan BIN-TMP-004. Tarrowen Mining Services is the haul contractor and its technical services group configures the collision awareness system (CAS). Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical employed the light vehicle driver.

Location and conditions

The main ramp at RL 312 runs approximately north-west on a 9.1 per cent descending grade and is 24 m wide between windrows. Traffic keeps left, so a descending truck runs on the open, pit side of the road. The RL 312 spur joins the ramp on a descending truck's left, on the inside of a left-hand bend, at an included angle of 71 degrees and 34 m below a convex grade break that the crews call the crest. The ramp surface was dry and well maintained. The wind was south-east at 8 km/h, the temperature was 9 degrees and there was no precipitation. It was dark: there is no fixed lighting in the Stage 4 pit, and moonset was at 23:18 the previous evening.

Vehicles and people

HT-407 was commissioned in 03/2021 and had 31,480 engine hours. Its last 500 hour service was on 28/07/2026. LV-118 was a 4WD utility in service since 02/2024 with 61,200 km. It was fitted with a certified roll-over protection structure, a 4.5 m amber beacon whip and a UHF radio. It was not dispatched, carried no fleet management system (FMS), and had a passive CAS tag.

The haul truck operator had 14 months at Bindarra and 7 years on 220 t class rigid haul trucks. The operator was on night 10 of a 14 night swing and was 8 hours 47 minutes into a 12 hour 30 minute shift. The light vehicle driver was on the third of three night shifts at Bindarra, having been issued a site access card on 09/08/2026. The night shift supervisor had 2 years 6 months in the role and supervised the haul fleet, excavators, ancillary fleet, dozers and dispatch operator for Stage 4.

Events before the shift

A works order, WO-26-4471, raised on 28/07/2026, provided for 240 m of access road to dewatering bore DW-14 at RL 312, and the works were completed on 31/07/2026. The spur was opened to light vehicles on 02/08/2026, when the bore was energised. The "ROAD CLOSED - CONSTRUCTION" sign at the spur mouth was removed the same day and nothing was installed in its place. The intersection carried no warning sign on either ramp approach, no give-way or stop control, no delineation and no posted speed for the spur.

At about 22:10 on 04/08/2026 a dewatering technician came out of the spur in front of a descending haul truck about 60 m away, reversed back into the spur and let the truck pass. The technician submitted hazard report HAZ-2026-0917 at 23:48 that night. It described the rise in the ramp, the windrow, the absence of a sign on the ramp and of a give-way on the spur, and the technician's view that the trucks did not know the road was there. The Dewatering Superintendent closed the report on 06/08/2026 with a reminder to the crew, and the risk rating was reduced from Medium to Low on closure.

The light vehicle driver's site access card was issued on 09/08/2026 after a 20 minute gatehouse briefing, and the driver's first night shift at Bindarra began that evening. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the Bindarra site-specific supplement was issued to the light vehicle driver]

The approach and the collision

The pit channel recording shows that dispatch called Stage 4 back to work from crib at 02:22:41. HT-407 then completed a loaded cycle to the ROM pad and called at each listed intersection it passed, and each call was acknowledged. At 02:46:21 it called at the RL 360 crossover, going down empty.

The light vehicle driver finished a set of levels at the DW-14 collar and drove the 240 m spur towards the ramp, leaving the collar at about 02:45 and reaching the mouth at about 02:47. These movements rest on the driver's own account, and [NOT ESTABLISHED: finalised interview with the light vehicle driver, whose account is relied on for the spur approach]. The driver said the vehicle was slowed at the mouth, that the driver looked right up the ramp, saw nothing and drove out at about 25 km/h, turning right to go back up the ramp. The driver did not believe the vehicle had come to a complete stop. The night shift supervisor did not know a light vehicle was in the pit.

The truck was descending empty at 37 km/h. The fleet management system download shows the last steady data point at 02:47:06.0, with the truck 53 m above the spur mouth, which is where the survey places the first sight of the light vehicle's beacon over the crest. The in-cab road network, last published on 24/07/2026, showed the main ramp with no intersection at RL 312. The haul truck operator described coming over the crest, seeing a glow on the road, and then the whip coming up over it. The operator estimated the distance at about 40 m, while the survey measure is 53 m.

At 02:47:07.4, 1.4 seconds after that data point, service brake pressure rose from 0 to 620 kPa in 0.4 seconds, the retarder went to maximum and 14 degrees of right steering was applied. The CAS logged a proximity event at 02:47:09.2 at a range of 21.4 m and 32 km/h closing, with the light vehicle at the spur mouth. The alert was suppressed by a geofence and nothing was presented in the cab. The haul truck operator said later that the CAS had never sounded on that part of the ramp in 14 months.

The impact occurred at 02:47:12.0 at 24 km/h, 6.2 m into the ramp from the spur mouth and 3.1 m out from the toe of the inner windrow. The light vehicle was turning right across the descending lane, with its right side towards the truck. The truck's front left struck it, and the accelerometer logged 1.9 g longitudinal. The light vehicle was pushed 18.4 m down the ramp, going over at about 11.2 m, and came to rest on its left side against the inner windrow, facing down-ramp. HT-407 stopped at about 02:47:19, 19 m below the intersection.

Damage and injuries

The light vehicle was destroyed. Its roll-over protection structure was deformed inward at the right rear mounting but was not breached, and the driver's seatbelt was fastened with loading marks on the webbing. The truck's damage was confined to the front left bumper, the left mudguard and the lower two steps of the access ladder, and it returned to service on 14/08/2026. The light vehicle driver sustained a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax, and was conscious throughout. [NOT ESTABLISHED: injury status of the haul truck operator]

The response

The haul truck operator made the first radio call at 02:47:41 and a second at 02:47:52 requesting the emergency response team (ERT). At 02:48:01, 49 seconds after the collision, dispatch stopped all Stage 4 traffic and told the operator to stay in the cab until the ramp was stopped above and below. Dispatch released the operator at 02:48:44. The operator then went down to the driver and stayed until the response team arrived, and reported that the driver was conscious and could not get out because the door was against the ground. The night shift supervisor, who was at the ROM pad, told the operator by radio not to move the driver, and reached the scene about five minutes later.

Dispatch paged the emergency response team at 02:48. The first response vehicle entered the pit at 02:51 and reached the scene at 02:54. The night shift carries one qualified mines rescue paramedic, who was at the surface medical facility. The second responder, who must be present before any extrication, is called from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse and arrived at 03:07 with the hydraulic rescue tool. The driver was extricated through the rear of the vehicle at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision, reached the surface medical facility at 03:41 and was flown to the metropolitan trauma centre at 07:40. The post-incident review recorded that the paramedic's primary survey was complete and the extrication plan made at 02:58, that the extrication was delayed by approximately 9 minutes waiting for the second responder and the tool, and that the delay did not affect the clinical outcome on this occasion. How the extrication arrangement bears on the occurrence is still being examined.

Immediate actions

The Stage 4 pit stood down for 9 hours 15 minutes, and the main ramp below RL 340 was closed for 22 hours. The RL 312 spur was barricaded and closed to all traffic. Both vehicles were isolated and left in position, and the scene was photographed and surveyed before recovery. The haul truck operator and the night shift supervisor were stood down for the rest of the shift and both drug and alcohol tests were negative. [NOT ESTABLISHED: drug and alcohol test result for the light vehicle driver] The contractor's technical services group downloaded the FMS and CAS data from HT-407 at 09:30 and provided it to the investigation unopened. At 05:10 the Mining Manager directed that a positive call on the pit channel be made before entering any intersection in the Stage 4 pit, whether listed in the plan or not, until further notice.

Analysis

This analysis follows the RL 312 intersection from its creation under a works order to the collision. It takes the controls that were absent first, then the conditions on the night, then the other factors that increased risk, and the matters examined without a settled result last.

What worked

Several defences performed as intended. The haul truck operator braked and steered right within 1.4 seconds of the beacon coming into view, inside the 1.5 seconds the traffic management plan's own stopping distance calculation allows. Service brake pressure rose from 0 to 620 kPa in 0.4 seconds, and the braked scuff deviated 1.4 m to the right over its first 20 m, away from an open side where the drop was more than 100 m. The impact speed was 24 km/h, against 37 km/h had no braking been applied. The truck's brakes had tested at 0.80 m/s2 on 03/08/2026 and tested at 0.82 on 14/08/2026, and the occurrence download gave 0.78.

The light vehicle's seatbelt was found fastened and its roll-over protection structure was deformed inward at the right rear mounting but was not breached, so both defences held. The night shift supervisor described the dispatcher's handling of the emergency positively. The dewatering technician who met a descending truck at the same spur on 04/08/2026 reversed out of its path and wrote up the near miss the same night.

Organisation

How the intersection existed without controls

Management of Change procedure ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.2 requires a management of change record before a change to the mine's road network. Clause 5.3 excludes "routine earthworks carried out under a works order within an approved pit design, where no new plant or vehicle type is introduced." Works order WO-26-4471 cut 240 m of access to bore DW-14 at RL 312, classified the work as routine earthworks within the approved Stage 4 design, recorded management of change as not required, and left its handover field reading "N/A". The case therefore met the exclusion on its face, and the works order form at Schedule 4 has no fields for referral of any kind.

The three referrals that clause 5.4 attaches to a management of change record were consequently not made. These were referral to the traffic management plan owner, to the survey department for the fleet management system road network, and to the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system geofences. The in-cab road network published on 24/07/2026 stayed current and showed the main ramp with no intersection at RL 312, and the S4-LOAD suppression geofence, carried up the ramp on 09/06/2026, already covered the place where the spur joined it. The pattern was not confined to this road. Of the 14 new roads cut in Stage 4 since the 12/11/2025 review, the 3 raised under a management of change record were referred to the plan's owner and the 11 raised under a works order were not.

It is very likely that opening the spur under a works order contributed to the absence of a stop control and signs and to the suppression of collision alerts at the intersection. A management of change record would have sent the new intersection to the plan's owner with a survey, and to the technical services group who configure the geofence, and the three roads raised that way were referred. The remaining allowance is that a referral is not itself a control, because the plan's owner might have left the spur to the annual review, and no out-of-cycle review has been held in the plan's eleven years.

Why the spur had no stop control or sign

Plan BIN-TMP-004 clause 6.2 applies to every intersection, listed or not. It requires available sight distance not less than the stopping distance of the largest vehicle at the posted speed and in no case less than 120 m, and where that cannot be achieved it requires a stop control, signalised control or traffic controller. The survey gave 41 m against a stopping distance of 96 m, so the second limb applied. Clause 6.4, which requires a warning sign 50 m in advance on each approach, a give-way control on the minor road and delineation at the mouth, applies only to intersections shown on the Schedule 1 road layout drawing, and the spur is not on it. The "ROAD CLOSED - CONSTRUCTION" sign at the mouth was removed on 02/08/2026, the day the spur was first used, and nothing was installed in its place. On the night the intersection had no warning sign on either approach, no stop or give-way control, no delineation and no posted speed.

It is likely that the missing stop control and signs contributed to the light vehicle driving out without stopping. A stop control would have held the light vehicle at the mouth while the truck came into its view, and a warning sign would have told the haul truck operator an intersection lay below the crest. The operator said in interview: "If there'd been a sign on my side of that crest I'd have been at twenty and I'd have been looking for him." The technician who came out of the same spur on 04/08/2026 reversed back and let the truck pass. The contrary evidence is that from the mouth the windrow and the grade break give 38 m, about four seconds of a truck at 37 km/h, which is a thin margin even from a standstill. The light vehicle driver was already slowing and looking, and the effect of a sign on the truck rests on the operator's own account after the event. A sign at an intersection absent from the in-cab map would also have been a single cue. These points limit how far the control can be said to have mattered, and they are the reason the judgement is held at likely rather than higher.

Why no call was made

Clause 4.3.2 of the plan states: "At intersections not listed at Appendix B, vehicles shall give way in accordance with clause 4.1. No call is required." Appendix B lists nine intersections. It is reissued only at the annual review, and an intersection is added only where it appears on Schedule 1 and the review assesses it as requiring positive communication. Annual reviews were completed on 14/11/2023, 10/11/2024 and 12/11/2025, and no out-of-cycle review has been held under clause 9.1 in the plan's eleven years. No provision allows an intersection to be added between reviews, and none requires a new road to be referred to the plan's owner. The spur was on neither document, so no call was required of either driver.

The pit channel recording shows the practice matched the document. HT-407 called, and was acknowledged, at the RL 360 crossover at 02:28 going up and at 02:46:21 coming down, 51 seconds before the collision, and at the ROM pad turn-off at 02:37. It made no call at the spur. LV-118 made no transmission after logging on at 18:04. The haul truck operator, the light vehicle driver and the night shift supervisor each described the same practice, that calls are made at the nine listed intersections and nowhere else. The supervisor added that they had never corrected anybody for not calling elsewhere and that requiring calls everywhere would make the channel unusable.

Mines Safety Guideline MSG-14 shaped this arrangement without causing it. Clause 3.2 requires a review after "any significant change to the mine's road network" and neither defines the term nor gives an example. Clause 5.1 requires the operator to nominate positive-call intersections and sets no minimum and no basis for the nomination. Clause 3.5 leaves the plan a site document that is not approved by the Inspectorate. The guideline made doing nothing the default for both the review trigger and the listing, and it is likely that these gaps contributed to positive calls being required only at listed intersections and added only at the annual review. The evidence against is real. Bindarra's plan met the guideline on its face, having been reviewed inside twelve months and nominating nine zones, so the mine was not in breach. A site could hold an out-of-cycle review under its own clause 9.1 at any time, and nothing in the guideline prevents a mine listing every intersection it has. On that reading the organisational omission accounts for most of the effect and the external clause is background, so the judgement on the guideline is held at the standard of proof and no higher.

It is very likely that the restriction of positive calls to listed intersections contributed to neither driver making a call. Had RL 312 been listed, the operator would very likely have called, because the operator called at every listed intersection passed that night and the channel was open with the light vehicle on it. The remaining allowance is that a call made and not acknowledged still leaves a driver deciding whether to go. The absence of a call itself is also a factor the evidence supports. It is likely that the absence of a call from either vehicle contributed to neither driver being aware of the other, because a call from either would have been heard by the other, by dispatch and by the supervisor. It is discounted from certainty because a call gives knowledge and not separation, and the two vehicles would still have had to resolve who went first over 41 m of sight line.

Why the system gave no alert

The collision awareness system on the Stage 4 haul fleet operates at Level 8, operator advisory. Level 9 intervention is available on the fleet and is not enabled at Bindarra. Advisory alerts are raised when a tag enters the 60 m ring above a 10 km/h closing rate, except inside a suppression geofence, where no alert is raised at any range and a proximity event is logged only once the range falls below 25 m. The S4-LOAD geofence was drawn around the loading face on 14/03/2025 to stop nuisance alerts and was extended northward on 09/06/2026 when the face advanced. That carried the boundary up the main ramp for the first time, to a point 180 m up-ramp of the RL 312 intersection, so the spur, cut from 28/07/2026, joined the ramp inside the suppressed area. The configuration holds only the new boundary. [NOT ESTABLISHED: size of the geofence extension] The contractor's technical services group made the extension as a system configuration task, and it was not recorded in the traffic management plan or reviewed against it.

The system logged a proximity event at 02:47:09.2 at 21.4 m with 32 km/h closing, and the alert was suppressed. In the twelve months before the occurrence HT-407 raised 1,684 advisory alerts, every one outside the geofence and none inside it. Across the fleet 68 proximity events inside it were suppressed, nine of them a light vehicle on the main ramp below the boundary, all after 09/06/2026. These events were recorded and visible in the system, but the standing report covers alert counts and system health and does not report suppressions, so nobody had looked. No training record anywhere on site, for any person, covers the geofences. The haul truck operator said in interview: "I assumed there was nothing to go off at." The operator also said: "Nobody ever told me it's switched off down there." The night shift supervisor knew the system was off at the dig from about the middle of 2025, but did not know the geofence had been extended in June 2026 or that it reached the ramp.

Two readings of influence were weighed. On one, the operator had learned over fourteen months that a quiet system on the ramp meant an empty ramp. For the first ten of those months that was true because the ramp lay outside the geofence, and from June the system was silent there whatever was on the road. The expectation gave the operator one less reason to think anyone could be there on a ramp that showed no intersection on the operator's screen and none on the road. On the other reading, the alert would have bought little. Unsuppressed, it would have sounded when the tag entered the 60 m ring at about 02:47:06.5, half a second after the beacon came into view and about a second before the brakes went on. The system is advisory only, and the expectation is not shown to have changed what the operator did, since the operator was descending at the speed operators use on that ramp and named a sign, not the system, as the remedy. It is likely that suppression of the alerts by a geofence operators knew nothing of contributed to neither driver being aware of the other until the truck came over the crest, through the expectation and not through the timing of the alert. The effect is real and cannot be measured, and the judgement is held at the standard of proof and no higher.

Why the driver was driving in the pit

Contractor Management Standard ORR-STD-009 clause 7.3 allows a contractor's own general induction to be accepted as equivalent where a recognition agreement is held, and Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical has held one since 2023. Clause 7.4 states that equivalence does not extend to the Bindarra site-specific supplement or to the light vehicle pit driving assessment, which every person who will drive in an operating pit must complete at site. Clause 7.5 makes the engaging department responsible for verifying this before a card is issued. The gatehouse issued the card on 09/08/2026 against the recognition agreement alone after a 20 minute briefing on muster points, speed limits and personal protective equipment. It holds no record of either item and is not asked for one, and nothing in the access card system distinguishes a person who may drive in an operating pit from one who may not. The driver's training file records the Hallorn online module of 24/07/2026 and no pit driving assessment. The driver had never heard of the assessment and had never seen the traffic management plan. No record shows the site supplement being issued, completed or signed for. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the Bindarra site-specific supplement was issued to the light vehicle driver]

It is likely that issuing access cards without checking the pit driving assessment contributed to the light vehicle driving out of the spur without stopping. The assessment is where a light vehicle driver is taught how to approach an intersection that cannot be seen up, which is to stop and look again and not merely to slow, and on the recorded times a stop at the mouth would very likely have shown the driver the truck. The evidence against is that the driver was already applying the first rule the assessment teaches, that light vehicles give way to heavy vehicles at all times, and the driver slowed and looked before going. The plan requires no call at an unlisted intersection, so the assessment would not have taught a call at RL 312, and the driver's statement that the driver would have called if told to cannot be extended that far. [NOT ESTABLISHED: content of the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment]

Context from hazard reporting

The hazard reporting history gives context for how the conditions persisted but is not a tested factor. Hazard report HAZ-2026-0917, submitted at 23:48 on 04/08/2026, described the rise, the windrow, a truck about sixty metres away, no sign and no give-way. It said: "The trucks are doing forty coming down empty. I do not think they know the road is there." The Dewatering Superintendent closed it on 06/08/2026 with a reminder to the crew to take care and give way, reduced the rating from Medium to Low, and did not refer it to the mining department, the contractor, the survey department or the plan owner. Three further reports from 03/2025, 09/2025 and 02/2026, at three other locations, each described a light vehicle and a haul truck meeting unexpectedly at an unlisted intersection, and each was closed with a reminder to the crew. None resulted in a change to Appendix B, Schedule 1 or a physical control. [NOT ESTABLISHED: any tested factor for the closure practice on hazard reports]

Environment

The convergence at the crest

The spur mouth lies 34 m below a convex grade break, which the crews call the crest. The survey gave the descending operator, at an eye height of 5.80 m, line of sight to the spur mouth at 41 m, and to the top of the 4.5 m beacon whip of a light vehicle approaching the mouth at 53 m. A driver at the mouth, at an eye height of 1.45 m, first has line of sight to a descending truck at 38 m, and the 1.6 m inner windrow takes the truck's lower body out of view for the last 25 m of the spur's approach. The stopping distance of the empty truck at the posted 40 km/h on the 9 per cent descent is 96 m on the manufacturer's data with a 1.5 second response, and about 68 m on brakes alone from 37 km/h at the recorded 0.78 m/s2. A truck at the posted speed therefore could not stop for anything first seen at 53 m. With twice the sight line, the same 1.4 second response and the same braking would have stopped the truck short of the spur. It is very likely that the 41 m sight line contributed to neither driver being aware of the other until the truck came over the crest. The remaining allowance is that a sight line is fatal only once something is in it, and the other factors in this analysis put something there.

The haul truck operator said in interview that the whip came up at about forty metres. The survey places the first sight at 53 m, which is also where the download has the truck at its last steady data point. The operator's figure is an estimate of a distance seen for a second, and the survey is the measure.

People

The light vehicle's exit from the spur

The driver's account, corrected on read-back from stopped to slowed, is that the driver slowed at the mouth, looked right up the ramp, saw nothing and drove out, turning right to go back up the ramp. The driver put the speed coming out at about 25 km/h and does not believe a complete stop was made. The collision awareness log places the light vehicle at the spur mouth at 02:47:09.2 with the truck 21.4 m above it, and the impact was 2.8 seconds later, 6.2 m into the ramp. The truck was within the driver's 38 m of view from about 02:47:07.4, nearly two seconds before the mouth was reached, so the look came when the truck was beyond anything the position let the driver see. The driver's own estimate of the time, about ten to three, is later than the recorded collision and is not used. The movements before the mouth rest on the driver's account alone.

It is extremely likely that the light vehicle driving out of the spur without stopping contributed to neither driver being aware of the other until the truck came over the crest, because without the light vehicle on the ramp there is no collision. Had the driver stopped at the mouth and looked again, the truck was already inside the view from there, and the driver would very likely have seen it and let it pass, as the technician did on 04/08/2026. The remaining allowance is that a stop is only as good as the look from it, at 38 m.

Neither driver aware of the other

HT-407 was descending empty at 37 km/h with no intersection on its in-cab map, no warning sign, no call and no alert. LV-118 was leaving the spur towards a mouth with 38 m of sight line, no give-way control, no call and no knowledge of the truck. The night shift supervisor did not know a light vehicle was in the pit, and no permit, call-in or board exists by which the supervisor could have known. The supervisor described not being told which light vehicles were in the pit and proposed a permit, a call-in or some record by which the supervisor of an operating pit knows which light vehicles are in it. Neither the radio log, the download, the collision awareness log nor any of the three interviews contains an indication that either driver knew of the other before the beacon appeared. It is extremely likely that the convergence of the two vehicles, each unknown to the other until about six seconds remained, contributed to the collision, which followed directly and could not be prevented in the time left.

Equipment

Impact and injury

The truck's front left struck the right side of the light vehicle at 24 km/h, 4.6 seconds after the brake application and 6.2 m into the ramp from the spur mouth, 3.1 m out from the toe of the inner windrow. The accelerometer logged 1.9 g longitudinal. Damage to LV-118 was concentrated on the right side from the B pillar forward, and damage to HT-407 was confined to the front left bumper, the left mudguard and the lower two steps of the access ladder. A continuous gouge ran 18.4 m down-ramp, changing at 11.2 m from tyre scuff to body panel gouge, which is where the vehicle went over, and right-side glass and mirror fragments lay from 4.8 m to 14 m down-ramp. The steering to the right towards the wall kept the push running down the ramp, so the vehicle came to rest against the pit side windrow and was not driven through it. The impact is virtually certain to have been the mechanism by which the convergence became an injury, and the roll-over is virtually certain to be how the collision produced the fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and small pneumothorax that make this a serious occurrence.

Other factors that increased risk

Roster as a standing exposure

The contractor's Stage 4 haul roster is 14 nights on and 7 off, 18:00 to 06:30, a 12 hour 30 minute shift with a 30 minute crib, inside a fatigue management standard that permits up to 14 consecutive night shifts with a minimum 10 hour break. Every limit in the standard was met, and the previous nine shifts were worked in sequence with none extended beyond 12 hours 40 minutes. The collision was 8 hours 47 minutes into the shift of night 10, inside the window of lowest circadian alertness. The roster did not contribute to this occurrence, and it is unlikely that it did. The one mechanism it could have worked through, a slow response, is contradicted by the download, which gives 1.4 seconds from the beacon coming into view to a brake pressure rise, inside the plan's own allowance, with correct and immediate braking and steering. Braking at 0.78 m/s2 from 53 m, a response time of zero still ends in a collision, at about 17 km/h instead of 24. The 1.4 seconds cost about 7 km/h of impact speed, not the collision.

The roster nevertheless increased risk. It is likely that it was a risk worth acting on, because it puts every haul truck operator at the wheel of a 220 tonne vehicle in the small hours of a tenth, twelfth and fourteenth consecutive night on every swing, where the defence against an unlit hazard at an unlisted intersection is the operator's own detection and response. At an intersection with a longer sight line than RL 312, a slower response could be the difference between stopping and not.

Extrication timing

The Bindarra night shift is rostered with one qualified mines rescue paramedic at the surface medical facility. The second responder, who must be present before any extrication is begun, is called in from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse, in the second response vehicle that carries the hydraulic rescue tool. Dispatch paged the team at 02:48, the first response vehicle entered the pit at 02:51 and reached the scene at 02:54, and the second responder arrived with the tool at 03:07. The driver was extricated through the rear of the vehicle at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision. The post-incident review measured a delay of approximately 9 minutes, from 02:58, when the paramedic's primary survey was complete and the extrication plan made, to the second responder's arrival. It recorded that the delay did not affect the clinical outcome because the injuries were stable and the patient was conscious throughout.

The collision and the injuries were complete before the response was paged, so on the evidence so far the response time is unlikely to have affected the occurrence or its outcome. The arrangement is still a matter of risk. It is very likely that it would be a significant gap for a more severe casualty, because it applies on every night shift and nothing in it scales with the severity of what has happened. This matter is still being examined and is described at the strength its tests record so far.

Matters examined and not settled

Airborne dust above the intersection

Airborne dust on the ramp above the intersection was examined. On the evidence so far it is likely that dust was present during the truck's approach, and whether it affected the operator's sighting is about as likely as not. For its presence, the water cart's last pass on that section was at 01:10, 1 hour 37 minutes before the collision against a standing 90 minute interval, so a pass was 7 minutes overdue. The fixed monitor on the RL 328 bench, 180 m up-ramp of the intersection and above the grade break the truck came over, logged PM10 at 142 micrograms per cubic metre between 02:40 and 02:50, against a shift mean of 88. The haul truck operator described dust hanging on the ramp, said the cart had been through earlier and that the ramp dries out, and the descent was behind the truck's own lights into an unlit pit.

The case against is strong. The reading of 142 is well below the site trigger of 250 and measures particulate at a monitor head, not what could be seen from either cab. The light vehicle driver was firm that the air was clear, although this described the spur below the windrow, slow or stopped, and not the ramp above the crest where the truck was. The beacon was in view from 53 m, the first point the survey says it could be seen at all, and the download puts the truck there at its last steady data point, so a sighting at the geometric limit leaves dust nothing to explain. The operator declined to say it made a difference, and a 1.4 second response from that point, inside the plan's allowance, leaves no room for a delay to hide in. The matter could not be settled because the sighting is inferred from the last steady data point and the survey and is not recorded, so a fraction of a second lost at the edge of the lights cannot be excluded. [NOT ESTABLISHED: measurement of what could be seen from either cab on the night] It remains unresolved.

Haul truck operator fatigue

Whether the haul truck operator was fatigued to a degree that degraded performance during the approach was examined and could not be settled, and the evidence is evenly balanced. In favour, the operator was on night 10 of 14, 8 hours 47 minutes into a 12 hour 30 minute shift, inside the window of lowest circadian alertness. The operator's voluntary sleep record gives between 5 and 7 hours on each of the ten days before, 6 hours 30 minutes on the last. The operator said in interview that they were tired "the way you are on night ten", and the task, detecting a hazard in an unlit pit, is the one fatigue degrades first.

Against it, the operator also said "Not falling asleep tired", and every limit in the contractor's fatigue standard was met. The recorded performance shows none of the usual signs, with a 1.4 second response inside the plan's 1.5 seconds and braking and steering that were correct and immediate. Being tired on a tenth night is not the same as being fatigued to a degree that degrades performance, and only a detailed fatigue assessment would reach the question. [NOT ESTABLISHED: detailed fatigue assessment of the haul truck operator] Even had it been shown, a response time of zero would still have ended in a collision, at about 17 km/h instead of 24. The matter remains unresolved.

Hypotheses tested and excluded

Two hypotheses were examined and were not supported. It is very unlikely that the ramp surface was wet or slippery. The met station recorded no precipitation, the last rainfall was 26 days earlier, the water cart's last pass was at 01:10, and the investigator found the ramp dry throughout at 06:20. The braked scuff ran continuously for 58 m with no sign of a locked or sliding wheel, and the deceleration of 0.78 m/s2 was the figure the truck achieves dry. It is also very unlikely that the service brakes delivered less than their tested deceleration. The tests on 03/08/2026 and 14/08/2026 gave 0.80 and 0.82 against 0.78 in the occurrence, the pre-start check sheet for 11/08/2026 recorded no defects, and no brake, retarder or park brake defect had been raised in the previous twelve months.

Findings summary

The investigation applied the standard of proof "Likely or probable".

Contributing factors

  1. The traffic management guideline MSG-14 set no definition of a significant change and no basis for nominating positive-call intersections, which virtually certainly existed and likely contributed to the occurrence by making inaction the default for the plan's review and call list. (Safety Issue)
  2. The RL 312 spur was opened under a works order that classified the work as routine earthworks, so no management of change record was raised and nothing was referred to anyone. This virtually certainly existed and very likely contributed to the occurrence. (Safety Issue)
  3. Site access cards were issued with no check that the light vehicle pit driving assessment had been completed, which virtually certainly existed and likely contributed to the occurrence. (Safety Issue)
  4. The traffic management plan required positive calls only at the nine listed intersections and allowed an intersection to be added only at the annual review, which virtually certainly existed and very likely contributed to the occurrence. (Safety Issue)
  5. The collision awareness system alerts were suppressed at the spur by a geofence of which operators had not been told. This was very likely the case, and it likely contributed to the occurrence. (Safety Issue)
  6. The RL 312 intersection had no stop control or warning sign although it failed the plan's sight distance rule, which virtually certainly existed and likely contributed to the occurrence. (Safety Issue)
  7. The sight line at the spur was 41 m against a stopping distance of 96 m, which virtually certainly existed and very likely contributed to the occurrence.
  8. Neither driver made a positive call before entering the intersection, which virtually certainly occurred and likely contributed to the occurrence, although no call was required at an unlisted intersection.
  9. The light vehicle drove out of the spur onto the ramp without stopping, which virtually certainly occurred and very likely contributed to the occurrence.
  10. Neither driver was aware of the other until the truck came over the crest, which was very likely the case and very likely contributed to the occurrence.
  11. The front left of the haul truck struck the right side of the light vehicle at 24 km/h, which was virtually certain and virtually certainly contributed to the occurrence.
  12. The light vehicle was pushed 18.4 m down the ramp and rolled onto its left side, which was virtually certain and virtually certainly contributed to the occurrence.

Other factors that increased risk

  1. Haul operators were rostered for fourteen consecutive 12.5 hour night shifts. This virtually certainly existed, it was unlikely to have contributed to this occurrence, and it likely increased risk in general. (Safety Issue)
  2. The night shift extrication capability waited on a second responder called from the accommodation village, which virtually certainly existed. It was unlikely to have influenced this occurrence, and it very likely increased risk in general. (Safety Issue)

Other findings

  1. The haul truck operator braked and steered right within 1.4 seconds of the beacon coming into view. This virtually certainly occurred and very likely decreased the risk of a worse outcome, because it reduced the impact speed from 37 km/h to 24 km/h.
  2. It was very unlikely that the ramp surface was wet or slippery.
  3. It was very unlikely that the haul truck's service brakes delivered less than their tested deceleration during the stop.

Appendix B - Excluded hypotheses and matters not settled

Each matter below was examined. The two hypotheses that did not pass Existence testing are set out first, followed by the two matters whose tests did not settle.

Ramp surface wet or slippery at and above the intersection

This hypothesis was tested because an 18 m push down a 9 per cent grade raises a question about the surface. It was not supported, and its Existence test was recorded as very unlikely. Three independent sources agreed.

  • The met station recorded no precipitation on the night, and the last rainfall at the site was 26 days before the occurrence.
  • The water cart log put the last pass on that section at 01:10, 1 hour 37 minutes before the collision, against a standing instruction of a pass every 90 minutes. The investigator examined the ramp at 06:20 and found it dry throughout, with no damp patches, ponding or greasy film at or above the intersection.
  • The braked tyre scuff ran continuously for 58 m with no sign of a locked or sliding wheel. The mean deceleration of 0.78 m/s2 net compared with the unit's own tested 0.80 and 0.82 on the same dry grade.

Service brakes delivered less than their tested deceleration during the stop

This hypothesis was tested because a 220 tonne truck that does not stop in the distance available raises the brakes first. It was not supported, and its Existence test was recorded as very unlikely.

  • The monthly brake performance test on 03/08/2026, eight days before, gave a mean deceleration of 0.80 m/s2 net in the empty condition on a 9 per cent descending grade.
  • The test repeated on 14/08/2026, before the unit returned to service, gave 0.82 m/s2.
  • The download of the occurrence gave 0.78 m/s2 over the 4.6 seconds of braking, from 37 km/h to 24 km/h, which is within the scatter of the two tests.
  • Service brake pressure rose from 0 to 620 kPa in 0.4 seconds, and the retarder was at maximum throughout.
  • No brake, retarder or park brake defect was raised against the unit in the twelve months before the occurrence, and the pre-start check sheet for 11/08/2026 was complete and recorded no defects.

Airborne dust on the ramp above the intersection during the truck's approach

The investigation considered this matter and could not settle it. It is likely that elevated dust existed above the grade break the truck came over. The fixed dust monitor on the RL 328 bench, 180 m up-ramp of the intersection, logged PM10 at 142 micrograms per cubic metre in the ten minutes covering the occurrence against a shift mean of 88, and the last water cart pass was 7 minutes overdue. The haul truck operator described dust hanging on the ramp, and the descent was into an unlit pit. The light vehicle driver was firm that the air at the spur was clear.

Whether the dust affected the haul truck operator's detection of the light vehicle is about as likely as not. Against an effect, the reading of 142 is well below the site trigger of 250 and measures particulate at the monitor head, not what could be seen from a cab. The beacon was in view from 53 m, the first point at which the survey says it could be seen at all, and the response of 1.4 seconds from there was inside the 1.5 seconds the plan's stopping distance calculation allows. The haul truck operator declined to say that dust made a difference. For an effect, the truck's first sighting is inferred from the last steady data point and the survey and was not recorded, so the data cannot exclude dust costing a fraction of a second at the edge of the lights. Nothing at Bindarra measures visibility, and no measurement exists of what could be seen from either cab. The matter could not be settled on the evidence available.

Haul truck operator fatigued during the approach to the intersection

The investigation considered this matter and could not settle it. The matter was left unresolved at Existence, where the evidence is evenly balanced.

  • For fatigue: the operator was on night 10 of a 14 night swing and 8 hours 47 minutes into a 12 hour 30 minute shift, inside the window of lowest circadian alertness. The operator's own voluntary sleep record gave between 5 and 7 hours on each of the ten days before, and 6 hours 30 minutes on the last of them. The operator described being tired "the way you are on night ten", and detection in an unlit pit is the task fatigue degrades first.
  • Against fatigue: the operator described the tiredness as ordinary and said they were awake and driving properly. Every limit in the contractor's fatigue standard was met. The recorded response of 1.4 seconds from the beacon coming into view to a brake pressure rise was inside the 1.5 seconds the plan assumes, and the braking and steering were correct and immediate.

A reported tiredness on a tenth night is not the same as fatigue to a degree that degrades performance, and the recorded response argues against it, but no other evidence reaches the question. A detailed fatigue assessment would be needed to settle it, and none was carried out. Influence was not tested. Even with a response time of zero, braking at 0.78 m/s2 from 53 m would still have ended in a collision, at about 17 km/h instead of 24 km/h.

That precision is not supported by the estimated endpoints. The driver's own "about ten to three" is also later than the recorded collision at 02:47:12. - Distance at first sighting: the haul truck operator estimated about forty metres, in both the interview and safety report ASR-2026-0341. The survey and FMS download give 53 m. The investigator's note resolves this in favour of the survey. - Push distance: occurrence notification ORR-OCC-2026-0332 gives "approximately 18 m" and the scene examination gives 18.4 m. These are consistent, but the notification figure is rounded. - Truck rest position: the FMS download gives 19 m below the intersection. The braked scuff runs 58 m from a point 38.5 m up-ramp of the spur mouth, which implies about 19.5 m. This is a minor difference. - Timeline entry at 02:47:06 lists "Haul truck operator fatigued during the approach to the intersection" as a linked factor. No test category for that factor appears anywhere in the evidence provided, so its status cannot be determined from the material. - Light vehicle driver interview is not finalised. His account of slowing rather than stopping and his speed estimate of about 25 km/h are drawn from unfinalised notes, so the investigator should confirm them before release. - [Analysis] - Light vehicle drove out of the spur without stopping: the driver puts his exit speed at about 25 km/h, but the collision awareness system log places him at the spur mouth at 02:47:09.2 and the impact 6.2 m into the ramp 2.8 seconds later. That is an average of roughly 8 km/h. The CAS extract also treats the 32 km/h closing rate as the truck's own speed, which implies the light vehicle was close to stationary. The two need reconciling. - Light vehicle drove out of the spur without stopping, and Neither driver aware of the other: the driver says he looked at the mouth, but the analysis places his look "a second or two before the truck came over the crest" (about 02:47:04 to 02:47:05). He reached the mouth at 02:47:09.2, so his look on those times came several seconds before he reached the mouth, not at it. - Collision alerts suppressed at the spur: the evidence for influence says the system was correct for "the first ten" of the operator's fourteen months. His site induction was 06/2025 and the geofence was extended on 09/06/2026, about twelve months later. The ten months appears to be the statistics extract window (12/08/2025 to 09/06/2026), not his tenure. - Collision alerts suppressed at the spur: the spur is said to have been "cut from 28/07/2026". That is the date WO-26-4471 was raised. It was approved on 29/07/2026, and the FMS extract says the spur was "cut on 31/07/2026", which is the completion date. - Neither driver made a positive call: the evidence states LV-118 made no transmission all shift beyond logging on at 18:04. The listening period is described as running from the return from crib (02:22:41) to two minutes after the collision, and the radio extract covers 02:20 to 02:52 only. The whole-shift claim goes beyond the period recorded as reviewed. - Spur opened under a works order: the investigator note refers to "the owner's power to direct a call between reviews", but BIN-TMP-004 is recorded as containing no provision allowing an intersection to be added between reviews. The source of that power, and its relation to the 05:10 direction, is not stated. - Light vehicle leaves the bore collar (timeline): 240 m in about 2 minutes 06 seconds is an average of about 7 km/h. This sits uneasily with an exit speed of about 25 km/h, unless much of that time was spent stationary. The estimate's basis may need checking. - [Findings summary] - Ramp grade: the approved Event overview gives the descending grade at RL 312 as 9.1 per cent. The sight line, brake and surface objects record it as 9 per cent. The investigator may wish to confirm which figure the survey supports. - "Airborne dust on the ramp above the intersection" and "Haul truck operator fatigued during the approach to the intersection" were tested as Inconclusive and do not appear in the Findings scaffold. The difference may come from the turn geometry, or from the 6.2 m being a perpendicular measure, but it is worth checking that the estimate and the derived position agree. - Fatigue ("Haul truck operator fatigued during the approach to the intersection" and the checklist): The checklist answers "Yes" to "Is a detailed fatigue assessment required?", but the test note says a detailed fatigue assessment was not pursued.
